messages.body_plain:
Hi Allie,
your code should work just fine (assuming you are on a Windows machine). Just be aware that if you import your WMF to another application like PowerPoint, you need to "ungroup" the picture before you can edit it as vector object. Until you do that, it is rasterized and will behave like a raster graphics. Once you "ungroup" it, you will see it split into its components and, by further ungrouping them, you will finally be able to edit them one by one.
Hope this helps!
Best Regards,
Marco.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Allie,
thanks for posting those examples, I understand better what you mean now. So you get indeed a vector format (through WMF) but the problem is that the quality is not as expected, in particular the density curves of our violin plots are jagged.
I have 2 further suggestions you can try:
1) Use EMF instead of WMF. EMF should have more advanced capabilities in rendering curves. Not sure though if this really makes a difference on how the file is saved.
2) Try to scale up the dimension of your saved file by passing a width and height to ggsave() which are larger than the default ones. This should result in more points in your density curves and therefore - I assume - a smoother look.
3) Try both 1 and 2.
Best Regards,
Marco.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I would like to space the breaks on the x axis of a plot based on the
string width of some elements, but I fail to do so.

Assume, I want to use geom_text to 'draw' something table-like.

Here is a standard plot:

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
library("ggplot2")
library("plyr")
library("grid")

## generate some illustrative data
ppp <- data.frame(names=rep(c("a", "b"), 2),
                  values=c("dtrn",
                      "dtrns",
                      "updtruudtreundegxdtraenuglditrengdulhlb",
                      "uphldrso"),
                  factor=rep(c("x", "y"), each=2))

## the standard plot with probably overlapping text
ggplot(ppp, aes(x=factor, y=names)) +
    geom_text(aes(label=values), hjust=1)
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

I'd love to have
(a)  the second column at the right side of the plot
(b1) the widths of both columns to be just enough to fit the contents

Here is some first failing idea (continued example):

--8<---------------cut here---------------start------------->8---
## calc the right side of the 'columns'
colwidths <- dlply(ppp, .(factor), function(x) max(stringWidth(x$values)))
colends <- colwidths
colends$y <- colends$x + colends$y
ppp$colends <- rep(do.call(unit.c, colends), each=2)
## plot
ggplot(ppp, aes(x=colends, y=names)) +
    geom_text(aes(label=values), hjust=1)
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

I do understand that there are problems with my wish to force the x
breaks at specific positions.  So, I would be happy if
(b2) the x breaks are proportional to the stringWidths of the contents
     i.e. in the example the second column should get ~4 times as much
     space as the first column

How would I go to get (a) and (b1/2)?

If that is not (easily) feasible, I could plot the columns separately
and join the plots using gridArrange(), where I can easily pass a
widths argument.  But for that route, my question is how to get a
single column of the plot above properly right aligned, s.t. the second
column is at the right side of the plot.
scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0,0)) does not have the desired effect:

    geom_text(aes(label=values), hjust=1) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand=c(0,0))
--8<---------------cut here---------------end--------------->8---

Many thanks in advance for any pointers.

Regards,
Andreas

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have been made aware of your message by Andrew Heiss. I have found the same issue, and post a bug report:
https://github.com/hadley/ggplot2/issues/867

To pass this problem I created a small function to filter my dataset. When a single identifiant (in my case called iteration) has all his data equal, i make sure there is only one data:
#pre-treatment
#if all data are equal for one iteration, just put 1
for (iteration in unique(temp$iteration))
{
    values <- temp[temp$iteration == iteration,2]
    if (length(unique(values)) == 1 && length(values) > 1)
    {
        val <- unique(values)
        temp <- temp[! temp$iteration == iteration,]
        temp <- rbind(temp,data.frame(iteration = iteration, median = val))
    }
}

Jean-Marc

Hi Allie,
just for the sake of completeness:
- if you can ungroup a WMF in PowerPoint, it is indeed a vector. The message you receive when ungrouping is normal in PowerPoint.
- EMF files (where E stands for Enhanced) have more capabilities respect to WMF files. For example, EMF supports Bezier curves while WMF doesn't.
- A vector can indeed be scaled indefinitely once produced, but at the time you produce it the target size may make the difference as it scales the content and produces polygons with more points.
Anyway, I understand you are happy with your PNG based results, so the points above are just for future reference.
Best Regards,
Marco.

Hi:

You did not provide a reproducible example, so the one offered below
is a guess at what your intended example contains. From appearances,
the length of the two vectors fed as values in the scale functions are
the same length as the data points, so one option is to put those
values into the data frame itself prior to plotting. In my example
below, the colors appear to be unique, so I did not assign a factor to
it, even though you appear to have done so in your examples. OTOH,
since the shape values were repeated, it made sense to define a
corresponding factor. This way I could illustrate both
scale_identity() and scale_manual() and let you decide which one you
prefer.

library(ggplot2)

# Reproducible example (mod the random seed)
DF <- data.frame(x = rnorm(12), y = rnorm(12),
                 shpfac = factor(1:3, levels = LETTERS[1:3]),
                 col = c("#006633", "#009900", "#00FF66",

                              "#CC9900", "#FFCC00","#FFFF66",
                              "#003399", "#0066CC", "#0099CC",

                              "#9900CC", "#CC00FF", "#FF00FF"),
                 shp = c(15, 16, 17, 15,16,17,15,16,17,15,16,17))

ggplot(DF, aes(x = x, y = y, color = col, shape = shpfac)) +
   geom_point() +
   scale_color_identity() +
   scale_shape_manual(values = DF$shp)

By default, scale_identity() applies the aesthetic mapping in the plot
but does not create a legend guide. To include it, you need to add
guide = "legend" as an argument to the scale_color_identity call, but
the legend text values will be the hex codes. scale_identity()
directly maps the levels of the factor to the values of the
corresponding aesthetic.

Looking at your example again:

<snip>

> ggplot(graph_prox, aes(log_Ha_conv, PROX_MN))+
>   geom_point( aes(colour=factor (Scenarios)),size = 4)+
>   scale_color_manual(values=c("#006633", "#009900", "#00FF66",
>                               "#CC9900", "#FFCC00","#FFFF66",
>                               "#003399", "#0066CC", "#0099CC",
>                               "#9900CC", "#CC00FF", "#FF00FF"))+
>   scale_shape_manual(values = c(15, 16, 17, 15,16,17,15,16,17,15,16,17))

you have PROX_MN defined in the initial aes(), but did not assign an
aesthetic to it. Since there is no explicit mention of what is to be
associated with the shape aesthetic, I'm not surprised that ggplot2
ignored the scale_shape_manual() code and failed to plot distinct
shapes. If your intention was to map PROX_MN to shape and _assuming it
is a factor with three levels_, try something like this:

ggplot(graph_prox, aes(log_Ha_conv, shape = PROX_MN)) +
   geom_point( aes(colour=factor (Scenarios)),size = 4) +

   scale_color_manual(values=c("#006633", "#009900", "#00FF66",
                               "#CC9900", "#FFCC00","#FFFF66",
                               "#003399", "#0066CC", "#0099CC",
                               "#9900CC", "#CC00FF", "#FF00FF")) +

   scale_shape_manual(values = c(15, 16, 17))

If that doesn't work or the toy example above doesn't help, please
provide a reproducible example for the list to diagnose.

Dennis

In the example below, I want two legends which clearly give information about 2 different factors.  One legend should be for the "fill" and the other for the "color".

One solution, as I show, is to explicitly use layer().

But I think Hadley wrote that he might eventually deprecate the layer() function. (Also, explicit use of layer() is not well documented.) Is there another way to achieve the same result?

stuff<-data.frame(eks=1:10)
stuff$Why<-stuff$eks
stuff$GRUEP<-factor(with(stuff, ifelse(eks<5, "lo", "HI")))
stuff$EVENNESS<- factor( ifelse(((stuff$eks) %% 2)<1, "even", "odd"))
print(summary(stuff))
print(stuff)
library(ggplot2)

# Bad: Meaningless plot character in the "GRUEP" legend and meaningless black in the "EVENNESS" legend:

print(
 	ggplot(data=stuff, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=Why, fill=GRUEP, color=EVENNESS)) + geom_tile() + geom_point(shape=16, size=5)
 		+ scale_fill_manual(
 			values=c(
 				"lo"="yellow"
 				,
 				"HI"="pink"
 				)
 			)
 		+ scale_color_manual(
 			values=c(
 				"even"="green"
 				,
 				"odd"="red"
 				)
 			)
)

# Solution using layer():

layerGRUEP<-layer(
 	data=stuff
 	, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=Why, fill=GRUEP)
 	, geom="tile"
 	)
layerEVENNESS<-layer(
 	data=stuff
 	, mapping=aes(x=eks, y=Why, color=EVENNESS)
 	, geom="point"
 	)
print(
 	ggplot()
 	+ layerGRUEP
 	+ layerEVENNESS
 	+ scale_fill_manual(
 		values=c(
 			"lo"="yellow"
 			, "HI"="pink"
 			)
 		)
 	+ scale_color_manual(
 		values=c(
 			"odd"="green"
 			,"even"="red"
 			)
 		)
)

mydata$yvar <- factor(mydata$yvar,levels=c(8,4,6))

messages.body_plain:
Hi:

There are several ways you could go about this, but here's one attempt:

library(ggplot2)

# Create a factor to indicate output-pollutant combinations
cv2$set <- factor(rep(1:5, each = 2), labels = c("cardva-NO2", "cardva-NOx",
               "ami-PM25", "ami-PM10", "ischem-PM10"))

ggplot(cv2, aes(x = factor(group), y = pinc, color = pollutant)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lcinc, ymax = ucinc), width = 0.3, size = 1) +
    labs(x = "group") +
    facet_wrap(~ set, nrow = 1)

I decided to plot by group since Ozone is always in group 1 and the comparison
is always in group 2. My initial thought was to dodge by pollutant,
but the problem is
that since Ozone is always group 1 that the two Ozone error bars
always overlap in
group 1. The above was a compromise to ensure that each pair was being
plotted separately.

An alternative would be to use pollutant for the x-variable and try to
dodge by group, but
you run into the same overlap problem: Ozone is always group 1. There
are probably
better ways to do this, but since you didn't indicate the type of plot
you wanted this is one
shot at it.

The reason why I generated the set variable was because each pair of
groups was neither
associated with a unique outcome variable nor a unique comparison pollutant. By
combining the two, I was able to generate unique pairs. This seemed
reasonable to me
because Ozone was present in every pair and it wasn't immediately
clear why you would
want to compare the Ozone results against each other.

Dennis

from the ggplot2 book that has similar characteristics to what you
describe.

# Example using unemployment data from the economics data frame
# and the presidential data frame in the ggplot2 package

library(ggplot2)

# Monthly time series plot of unemployment rate

   geom_line() +
   labs(x = "", y = "No. unemployed (1000s)")

# Data on presidential terms over this time span
presterms <- presidential[-(1:2), ]

# Generated data to use for labeling terms
presmidterm <- data.frame(name = presterms$name, midterm =
   with(presterms, as.Date((as.numeric(start) + as.numeric(end))/2,
                               origin = "1970-01-01")),
   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
presmidterm$name[1] <- "Johnson"

ggplot() +
    theme_bw() +
    geom_rect(data = presterms, aes(xmin = start, xmax = end,
                  ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = party), alpha = 0.3) +
    geom_line(data = economics, aes(x = date, y = unemploy)) +
    labs(x = "", y = "No. unemployed (1000s)") +
    geom_text(data = presmidterm, aes(x = midterm, y = 2500, label = name),
               size = 3) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("blue", "red"))

Hi All,
I hope someone can help me to understand the weird behavior that I am seeing with e.g. stat_boxplot (i have the same problem when computing means using stat_summary).

I have a rather large dataset (420,000 rows x 20 columns). This is a nested design: 4 quarters - Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4 nested within 3 years - 2007, 2008, 2009. One column contains the Quarters and one the Years (both are factors). The remaining 18 columns each contain a different response variable - numeric or integer. For each response I want to construct a plot with facets - 3 facets (one for each year) each plot then containing four boxplots (one for each quarter).

My Goal was to be able to do this within a for loop - loop over the response columns (using mydata[,#] notation) - make the boxplots plot, use ggsave to save each plot - and i did this and it works - except that the statistics calculated for the boxplots are incorrect. There is a discrepancy between what ggplot plots and (what i obtain using ggplot_build) and what e.g. i compute using ddply (or in Excel).

However, if i make the same plot outside of the loop and access the columns in the dataframe by name e.g. 'Result' instead of 'mydata[,#]' then everything is fine. Similarly, if i make a new variable with all levels of Quarter x Year and don't facet by Year, then i can use the 'mydata[,#]' Notation and get boxplot statistics which match those from e.g. ddply or those i compute by hand in Excel.

As a work-around i am making the plots without faceting (using Quartal x Year on the x-axis) - but they are not as pretty and do not match the rest of my output, so it is not really an ideal solution. Moreover, i cannot understand what is even being computed by stat_boxplot when the mydata[,#] Syntax and facets are used ... and that makes me nervous.

I have made a reproducible example below which illustrates these three cases. Can someone explain to me why the 2nd case (test2) doesn't work how i expect? unfortunately, the syntax used in test2 is the best way i see to generate a series of plots quickly and painlessly. I've been struggling with this for days - and i really don't see where i am going wrong. but, i imagine that i must be overseeing something very basic

Hi:

If you want to apply the same type of plot to different variables in
your data frame, it's safer to wrap the plot 'n save inside a function
and then map it to the set of variables you want plotted. Here's an
example that extends your test data a bit:

# Note the way the data frame is constructed - cbind() is always a bad idea
# when the classes of the individual columns are not all the same
tobeplotted <- data.frame(Quartal = rep(c("Q1", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4"), 144),
                          Year = factor(rep(2007:2009, each = 4)),
                          Result1 = round(runif(576, 0, 20), 2),
                          Result2 = round(runif(576, 0, 10), 2),
                          Result3 = round(runif(576, 0, 5), 2))

library(plyr)
library(ggplot2)

# Compute the medians for each response by Year/Quartal combinations
qmed <- ddply(tobeplotted, .(Year, Quartal), numcolwise(median))
qmed

# Create a vector of response names
ynames <- paste0("Result", 1:3)

# Create a plot function. Note the use of aes_string(), which allows you to use
# quoted names on the right side of the assignment.

ebp <- function(y)
{
  p <- ggplot(data = tobeplotted, aes_string(x = "Quartal",
                      y = y, fill = "Year")) +
         geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0) +
         facet_wrap(~ Year)
  fname <- paste(y, "pdf", sep = ".")
  ggsave(fname, p)
}

# Recursively call the function for each name in ynames:
l_ply(ynames, ebp)

The medians match the results from ddply() in each case.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
Dear ggplot2 users,

I have recently developed a package, ggtern, for the generation of ternary diagrams, which have an additional axis and variable. My (partially incomplete) website can be found at ggtern.com <http://ggtern.com>, and, a case-study to demonstrate the capability can be found http://ggtern.com/case-study-zirconia-alumina-silica/:

The issue that I am having is that CRAN has rejected the package, since it accesses many ggplot2:::<xyz> internal variables and functions.

Dr. Wickham suggested that I post a question here, since some people may have a similar experience, or, know a workaround.

As an example, my package creates MANY new theme elements and inheritances, it firstly accesses the .element_tree (hidden within ggplot2), adds the new structures, then pushes it back to the ggplot2 namespace during the .onLoad() function call.

Here is a list of the internals that I use within this package, most simply get 'used' or referenced, however, there are a couple that get 'patched'.

PATCHED
ggplot2:::StatDensity2d
ggplot2:::GeomSegment
ggplot2:::StatSmooth
ggplot2:::.element_tree (for the new element structures)
ggplot2:::.all_aesthetics (Since I am making new 'aesthetic' mappings)

USED
ggplot2:::Geom    (The root proto environment when patching existing geometries)
ggplot2:::Stat       (Another proto environment when patching the stat-smooth.r function)
ggplot2:::set_last_plot  (Needed to patch print.ggplot, this is used in that function)
ggplot2:::el_def    (So I can define new 'theme' elements and ineritances)
ggplot2:::check_required_aesthetics
ggplot2:::coord_transform.cartesian
ggplot2:::train_cartesian

at least partially cut off at the top, but it's hard to tell without
an example...

messages.subject: Re: Clarification Regarding Usage Of "geom_bar"
messages.body_plain:
Hi:

Your problem illustrates the distinction between mapping and setting
aesthetics. A variable mapped to an aesthetic belongs in aes() or
aes_string(); setting an aesthetic to a constant value is done outside
of aes(). In your penultimate call, the following should work:

ggplot(diamonds) + geom_bar(aes(x = clarity, fill = cut), position = "fill")

'Mapping an aesthetic', means that different values of a variable are
associated with different values of an aesthetic. For example, you
might want to associate different point shapes or line types with
individual levels of a factor, so that would qualify as a mapping,
which would take place in aes(). OTOH, if you want to set color to be
blue or alpha transparency to be 0.3, that would be done outside of
aes(). In the above example, the fill aesthetic is mapped to cut,
which means different fill colors are associated with different levels
of cut; x and y variables (when relevant) are mapped, with rare
exceptions. In this call, you're setting position to be 'fill', so
that is specified outside of aes().

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, Dec 13, 2013 at 9:27 AM, Brian Diggs <brian....@gmail.com> wrote:
> On 12/12/2013 11:10 AM, Dennis Murphy wrote:
>>
>> Hi:
>>
>> Your problem illustrates the distinction between mapping and setting
>> aesthetics. A variable mapped to an aesthetic belongs in aes() or
>> aes_string(); setting an aesthetic to a constant value is done outside
>> of aes(). In your penultimate call, the following should work:
>>
>> ggplot(diamonds) + geom_bar(aes(x = clarity, fill = cut), position =
>> "fill")
>>
>> 'Mapping an aesthetic', means that different values of a variable are
>> associated with different values of an aesthetic. For example, you
>> might want to associate different point shapes or line types with
>> individual levels of a factor, so that would qualify as a mapping,
>> which would take place in aes(). OTOH, if you want to set color to be
>> blue or alpha transparency to be 0.3, that would be done outside of
>> aes(). In the above example, the fill aesthetic is mapped to cut,
>> which means different fill colors are associated with different levels
>> of cut; x and y variables (when relevant) are mapped, with rare
>> exceptions. In this call, you're setting position to be 'fill', so
>> that is specified outside of aes().
>
>
> This is a very good description of the difference between setting and
> mapping aesthetics, but in this case isn't relevant. `position` is not an
> aesthetic that could be mapped, so there is no case where it makes sense to
> be inside the `aes()` call. `position` is simply another argument to the
> `geom_bar()` function.

That was a major brain fart on my part. Thanks for the correction,
Brian! Indeed, positional adjustment is a separate concept from
aesthetics, and one can see this in the on-line help pages where
positional adjustment has its own subsection.

Dennis

messages.body_plain:
The arguments for geom_text are

args(geom_text)
function (mapping = NULL, data = NULL, stat = "identity", position = "identity",
    parse = FALSE, ...)

like most geom_* functions, the first argument is an aesthetic
mapping, usually created with aes. If you want to override the x and y
position mappings you can, but you are certainly going to have to name
them. Otherwise geom_text is going to assume that you've supplied the
arguments in order, i.e., that as.numeric(cityname$cit[1]) is the
mapping. Since this is an invalid mapping, it doesn't work. All this
to say that you just need to name your arguments:

p1  +    geom_text(x = as.numeric(cityname$cit[1]), y = 265, label =
"Large Cities")

Best,
Ista

Dear BHM,

Sure, of course.

Basically, I executed the following sequence when the new packages is loaded:

-----------------------------------------------------------------
#define a list of the names of all the internals that I need.
.internals <- c(".all_aesthetics", "set_last_plot", "coord_transform.cartesian", "train_cartesian", "scales_add_missing", "ggname", "new_panel", "train_layout", "map_layout", "map_position", "new_panel", "train_position","Stat","GeomPath","add_group","scales_transform_df","reset_scales","scales_train_df","scales_map_df","order_groups","TopLevel", "compute_intercept", "combine_elements","is.rel", "facet_render", "coord_labels", "xlabel", "ylabel", "element_render", "build_guides", "is.zero", "plot_clone", "set_last_plot", "add_theme", "make_labels", "update_guides", "zeroGrob", "el_def")
.internals <- unique(.internals) #just in case

#load from the ggplot2 namespace
ggint <- structure(
  mapply(function(.internals, i) getFromNamespace(i,"ggplot2"),.internals, .internals),
  class=c("internal")
)
-----------------------------------------------------------------

This creates a structure (ggint), containing duplicates of all internal functions/objects (as they appear in ggplot2), so, where I initially needed to call ggplot2:::<xyz> (and which was subsequently raising red-flags with CRAN), I can now call with ggint$<xyz>(...).

I ended up absolutely NOT being able to use assignInNamespace(...) in any way whatsoever, which is why I needed to bring so many of these internal functions forward, and, most of the above, were needed to successfully create a new theme_get() and theme_set() routines to address my need for new theme elements and heirarchies that were originally not defined in ggplot2.

Given the previous statement, any function that I initially wanted to patch (and made effective via assignInNamespace(...)), I needed to make a copy (including the desired patches) in the ggtern namespace, and this created a cascading effect in that any function which used the newly patched function in the ggplot2 namespace, also needed to be duplicated in the ggtern namespace, however, any time an internal object/function was used, it needed to be replaced by ggint$<xyz>, which is why the .internals list above is so lengthy.

Anyway, Hope this helps.

Regards,

Nick Hamilton.

messages.body_plain:
Borrowing from an idea of Winston Chang's posted a couple of years ago
in this group, here is a toy example that should illustrate what you
want:

DF <- data.frame(x = rep(c(1, 3, 4, 6, 10), each = 50),
                 y = sample(2:60, 250, replace = TRUE))

library(ggplot2)

ggplot(DF, aes(x = x, y = y, color = factor(x))) +
   geom_boxplot(aes(group = x)) +
   geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.04)) +
   geom_smooth(aes(group = 1))

The idea is that you group the unique x-values for the boxplots, which
should have a 1-1 correspondence with the variable mapped to color.
Notice the use of factor(x) for color to yield a discrete set for the
legend but otherwise x is numeric. You also need group = 1 for the
smooth since color is mapped discretely to x in the base layer.

Since you mentioned you have overlapping points in the data, there's a
chance that jittering points would be sufficient if you contain the
jitter width (and/or height). If you can jitter the points well, the
box plot is really unnecessary and is actually a bit of a distraction
if the point is to look at the relationship between bill length and
corolla length.

Dennis
